shipped_rows.title_o: Cross-Language Priming Asymmetries in Lexical Decision and Episodic Recognition

blind_target.title: Lexical acquisition and the modular lexicon.
blind_target.evidence_quote: In this final experiment, a more powerful test of the episodic L2 hypothesis is carried out using a more robust form of priming, namely, repetition priming rather than translation priming. As explained earlier, it has been found that in an episodic recognition task, old words show strong masked repetition priming, but there is no priming for new words (Forster, 1985; Rajaram & Neely, 1992).
blind_target.outcome_quote: The findings are clear. In an episodic recognition task, Chinese– English bilinguals show repetition priming for both old and new English (L2) words. This contrasts sharply with the results for the monolingual English speakers, where repetition priming was ob- tained for old words only.

prior_decision.quote: In this final experiment, a more powerful test of the episodic L2 hypothesis is carried out using a more robust form of priming, namely, repetition priming rather than translation priming. As explained earlier, it has been found that in an episodic recognition task, old words show strong masked repetition priming, but there is no priming for new words (Forster, 1985; Rajaram & Neely, 1992). This result was obtained with native English speakers, so the priming is L1–L1.
prior_decision.reason: Experiment 3 genuinely re-tests Forster's (1985) specific empirical finding—that in an episodic recognition task with native English speakers, studied ('old') words show strong masked repetition priming whereas unstudied ('new') words show no priming—by testing a new sample of 24 native English speakers alongside 20 Chinese–English bilinguals on old versus new English words in an episodic recognition task with masked repetition priming, and confirms the original finding in the native English speaker sample (significant priming for old items, M = 48 ms, p = .0001, and no significant priming for new items, M = 4 ms, p = .28; explicitly compared with Forster, 1985 in the Experiment 3 Discussion, lines 1969-1977).
